Short answer: The strongest correlates of PFOA (LBXPFOA) in NHANES are other PFAS measured in serum. Cross-chemical correlations outside the PFAS family are generally weak.

What tends to sit at the top
- PFOS (LBXPFOS): Spearman r typically ~0.6–0.8
- PFHxS (PFHxS; often LBXPFHS): ~0.5–0.7
- PFNA (LBXPFNA): ~0.5–0.7
- PFDA/DeA (perfluorodecanoic acid; code varies by cycle, e.g., LBXPFDE or LBXPFDA): ~0.4–0.6
- PFUnDA (LBXPFUN in some cycles): ~0.3–0.5
- MeFOSAA / EtFOSAA precursors (available in earlier cycles): ~0.4–0.7 when detection is good

What does not correlate much
- Urinary short–half-life chemicals (phthalate metabolites, phenols including BPA, PAH metabolites, organophosphate pesticide metabolites, many VOC metabolites): near zero correlations with serum PFOA in cross-sectional NHANES.
- Tobacco biomarkers (serum cotinine, urinary NNAL): near zero.
- Other persistent organics (PCBs, PBDEs) and metals: at most modest, often r ≤ 0.2–0.3; blood mercury sometimes shows small positive correlations that can reflect shared dietary sources (e.g., seafood), but these are not among the top correlates.

Cycle notes
- Exact ranks and magnitudes vary by NHANES cycle because of changing use patterns (e.g., PFOS/PFOA phase-outs), detection limits, and which PFAS were measured. Still, the top correlates of PFOA remain other PFAS in every cycle where the broader PFAS panel was assayed.

Bottom line
- Yes—the correlation structure for LBXPFOA is dominated by other PFAS compounds, consistent with shared sources, similar pharmacokinetics, and the same measurement matrix (serum). Non-PFAS environmental exposures rarely crack the top ranks and, when they do, correlations are modest. If you want a cycle-specific ranked list and coefficients, I can generate one for the cycles you care about.
